lecture19.title: Neuron, Neural Networks, LLMs and Agents

sections.title: Neuron, neural networks, LLMs and agents
From a neuron to agents that communicate

teaching.text: **A single neuron converts a list of inputs into one weighted sum, while a network converts an input vector into a decision vector.** Each layer combines the responses produced by the preceding layer, so the final responses can distinguish the possible answers.
children: The basic calculation is an inner product, multiplying inputs by weights and adding the products.

teaching.text: **A large language model processes a sequence of vectors and predicts the next item.** Its layers transform the representations until the output expresses a probability distribution over possible next tokens.
children: The example uses fifteen input vectors and predicts the sixteenth.

teaching.text: **An agentic system joins whole LLMs into a graph.** Different models outline, write, criticize, revise and finalize the response, and the revision can return to the critic for another evaluation.
children: The agents pass information to one another in English and can work in other human languages and computer languages.

teaching.text: **Inference processes the inputs with learned weights, while learning changes those weights.** Inner products support inference, and stochastic gradient descent changes the weights using the backward calculation organized through dynamic programming.

**A language model uses many layers because predicting the next word requires developing useful representations of the sequence.** Each layer receives the vectors produced by the previous layer and transforms them further.
children: The prediction depends on the representations produced by the whole sequence of processing stages.

teaching.text: **Several heads work in parallel within each layer.** The heads act as different experts whose contributions are brought together, allowing the layer to combine different information in its representations.
children: A head is a processing component inside the layer, and the experts are parts of the model rather than people supplying answers.

teaching.text: **The combined representations become the input to the following layer.** That layer again combines its heads’ contributions, so successive layers build on the work already done.
children: Parallel heads contribute within a stage, while successive layers develop the representations across stages.

sections.title: A dynamical rule across time and depth

teaching.text: **A dynamical system repeatedly transforms its current state into a new state.** An oscillator’s state contains position and velocity, and the output of an update becomes the starting point for the next update.
children: Position is updated using the old velocity, and velocity is then updated using the new position. The repeated alternation produces oscillation.

teaching.text: **Jordan’s recurrent network carries its recent output into the next moment.** Plan and state units feed the hidden layer, which produces an output that is copied back into the state units.
children: The state units also retain a fading trace through their self-connections. Reusing the same weights lets the network produce a sequence influenced by its recent history.

teaching.text: **The LLM comparison treats depth as a sequence of state changes.** One layer transforms the vectors, and the next layer transforms the resulting vectors again.
children: Following a single value through the layers gives a changing trajectory, although its curve is not a cosine.

teaching.text: **An oscillator or recurrent network reuses its rule across time, while the LLM has different weights at different layers.** The connection lies in how each new state develops from the preceding state.
children: Depth plays the role of time in the comparison, while each layer supplies its own transformation.

teaching.text: Different changing quantities can follow different trajectories over the same period. The stock-return sequences rise and fall along separate paths, so a trajectory describes how a quantity changes rather than requiring a particular curve such as a cosine.

sections.title: One prediction task for different sequences

teaching.text: An LLM reads **15 vectors** and has to guess the **16th**.
children: The question is what those vectors stand for.

teaching.text: They can be **words in a sentence**.
children: “The cat that the dog chased ran up the old tree and sat on the ___.”
The 16th vector is the **missing word**.

teaching.text: They can be **slices of sound** or **pieces of a picture**.
children: For a spectrogram, the 16th vector is the **next slice of sound**.
For a picture cut into squares, it is the **missing corner square**.

teaching.text: They can even be the parts of a **protein**.
children: Here they are the first **15 amino acids** of the insulin B chain.
The 16th vector is the **next amino acid**.

teaching.text: **The LLM only ever sees vectors.**
children: Words, sounds, pictures and molecules are all represented as vectors.
Each time, it answers one question, **what comes next?**

sections.title: Which sequences can be English words?

teaching.text: **Phonotactics is knowledge of which sound sequences a language allows.** English speakers use this knowledge without being explicitly taught each allowed sequence.
children: A simple English syllable can be a **consonant, a vowel, and a consonant**, as in Don, mat or fish.

teaching.text: Consonants can also come in **clusters**.
children: English allows split, flat and stop at the start of a word.
It allows desk, help and lamp at the end.

teaching.text: But only certain clusters are allowed, and **order matters**.
children: *lfat, *hepl and *lapm use the same letters as flat, help and lamp in the wrong order.
The allowed order flips around the vowel.

teaching.text: Long words are **chains of syllables**.
children: In At·lan·tic, t and l sit on two sides of a syllable break, so they are fine.
A word cannot start with tl, so *tlantic is impossible.
ng can end a syllable, as in ring, but cannot start one.

sections.title: Guessing the next letter reveals phonotactic knowledge

teaching.text: **Predicting the next letter uses knowledge of English sound and spelling patterns.**
children: The starts include ra_, sp_, skr_ and m_.

teaching.text: After a vowel, almost **any letter** can come next.
children: After ra_, the guesses are spread across many letters.

teaching.text: At the start of a word, the choices are **narrow**.
children: After sp_, b_ or f_, only l, r or a vowel can come next.
After skr_ or m_, only a vowel can come next.

teaching.text: Some letters can **never** come next.
children: English has no words starting with *spn, *skrl or *mb.

teaching.text: **Guessing the next letter is the same game an LLM plays.**
children: A GPT trained only on this game learns English sounds and spelling.
Its guesses are spread out after a vowel and focused on a few letters after skr_.

sections.title: Design an agentic system for English syllables

teaching.text: **Guessing a hidden word is how an LLM learns.** The model reads “The chef cracks the” and has to say what follows.
children: Every earlier word is a clue, so the hidden word depends on all of them. These relationships are **interdependencies**.

teaching.text: **The guess is a set of bets.** The model gives a probability to each possible word and puts the most on “egg.”
children: “Nut” and “code” get less because the earlier words make them less likely.

teaching.text: **Each revealed answer nudges the weights.** The change is small, and it makes the right word a little more likely next time.
children: The signal can hold sounds and images as well as words, and the learning works the same way.

sections.title: Text, speech and images in three different forms

teaching.text: **Only text arrives ready for the model.** Its words are separate pieces in a row, and each piece can become a vector.
children: “Now crack the egg” is four pieces.

teaching.text: **Speech and images arrive without any pieces.** Speech is one continuous change in air pressure, and an image is a grid of light.
children: Neither one has words in it.

teaching.text: **The model reads only rows of vectors.** Speech and images therefore have to be converted first.
children: The conversion gives each of them the same form as text.

sections.title: Speech becomes a row of frame vectors

teaching.text: **Cutting speech into frames gives it pieces.** A frame is a slice of sound about 20 milliseconds long.
children: The cuts fall at regular times.

teaching.text: **The speech encoder changes each slice into a vector.** It is a network trained on a large amount of audio.
children: One slice goes in and one vector comes out.

teaching.text: **A second of speech is 50 vectors in time order.** That row can be read like a sentence.
children: The earliest sound is first in the row.

sections.title: Images become a row of patch vectors

teaching.text: **Cutting an image into patches gives it pieces.** A patch is a small square of the image.
children: The egg image is cut into 16 patches.

teaching.text: **Reading order makes the patches a sequence.** They are taken left to right along the top and then along each line below.
children: A sequence has a first piece and a last piece, as a sentence does.

teaching.text: **The vision encoder gives one vector per patch.** Real systems use patches of 14 to 16 pixels and get hundreds of vectors from one image.
children: The example uses large patches only to stay simple.

teaching.text: **One row can hold all three senses.** Image patches, speech frames and words stand in a single sequence with the last word hidden.
children: The words are “Now,” “crack” and “the.”

teaching.text: **Clues cross from one sense to another.** A patch containing an egg and the sound of cracking both point to the hidden word.
children: These links are **cross-modal dependencies**.

teaching.text: **The model plays the same game.** It guesses the hidden piece from everything else in the row.
children: The earlier words still help, as they do in a row of text.

sections.title: Three cute puppies as an image, speech and words

teaching.text: **One event can be seen, heard and read.** “Three cute puppies” is an image, a spoken phrase and three written words.
children: The image is cut into 18 patches.

teaching.text: **The spectrogram is the spoken phrase laid out in time.** Higher means higher frequency, and darker means more energy.
children: Each thin column is a frame, and the words follow one another from left to right.

teaching.text: **Training places the three views in one row.** One piece of the row is hidden for the model to guess.
children: The same example is used for a hidden word, a hidden frame and a hidden patch.

sections.title: Training example 1 predicts the next word

teaching.text: **Words alone leave the model unsure.** After “three cute,” the bets on “kittens,” “puppies” and “babies” are close together.
children: Many endings fit those two words.

teaching.text: **The image and the sound settle the guess.** The image contains puppies and the sound contains the word, so the bet piles up on “puppies.”
children: These are clues from other senses.

teaching.text: **A good bet gives a small nudge.** The model bet 0.85 on the true word, so the error is small.
children: The weights move only a little.

sections.title: Training example 2 predicts a sound frame

teaching.text: **The model can also guess the next frame of sound.** It works through the sound from left to right, one frame at a time.
children: This is like teaching the model to speak a sentence it was given.

teaching.text: **The sound itself is the strongest clue.** The voice and the formants change smoothly, so recent frames say a lot about the next one.
children: The words give the next sound, the vowel in “pup,” and the image backs up the words.

teaching.text: **The error is the gap between guess and truth.** A frame is a column of energy values, one per frequency band.
children: The guess is close but not exact, and the gap nudges the weights.

sections.title: Training example 3 predicts an image patch

teaching.text: **The model can also guess the next patch of an image.** It works through the patches in reading order.
children: This is like teaching the model to draw what it was told.

teaching.text: **The clues give the content of the patch.** Two puppies are already drawn, “three” calls for one more, and “puppies” calls for dog ears.
children: The sound carries the same words as a backup.

teaching.text: **No clue gave the colour.** The guess takes the average colour of the first two puppies, but the third puppy is dark.
children: The colour is the biggest error, and it nudges the weights.

sections.title: Every piece can be the hidden one

teaching.text: **Each sense gives a clue for each kind of hidden piece.** That makes nine clues for a hidden word, a hidden frame and a hidden patch.
children: For a hidden word they are a plural noun, the word just spoken, and puppies in the image.

teaching.text: **A clue from the same sense says how the signal continues.** Grammar continues a sentence, smooth formants continue a sound, and fur and background continue an image.
children: These three are the same-sense clues.

teaching.text: **Clues from the other senses say what the thing is.** They say puppies, three of them.
children: Each sense fills gaps the others leave.

sections.title: Talking back, and what is new

teaching.text: **Speech output uses codes.** Sound is compressed into discrete codes that work like new words in the vocabulary.
children: The model predicts the next code as it predicts the next word.

teaching.text: **A decoder makes the codes audible.** It changes the row of codes back into a sound wave.
children: The model itself only predicts the codes.

teaching.text: **Three things are new.** They are a shared currency of vectors in one row, data where the senses appear together, and a schedule that protects what was already learned.
children: What stays the same is finding the dependencies in the signal.
